title: The Blacking Warehouse to the Abbey Floor: Dickens, the Roads of Kent, and the Instalment
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Portsea, born at Mile End Terrace
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Charles Dickens Letters Project chronology reads verbatim '(7 Feb.) Charles Dickens born at Mile End Terrace, Landport, Portsea'. The house number is disputed by the Portsmouth museum itself, 1 or 13 Mile End Terrace, and is left unresolved here. Coordinates are those of the surviving house at 393 Old Commercial Road, not the 2014 statue a kilometre south, with which several gazetteers confuse it.
stops.campa: A son is born at Mile End Terrace in Landport, on the Portsea side of Portsmouth, to John Dickens of the Navy Pay Office and his wife Elizabeth. They name him Charles John Huffam and baptise him at the parish church in March. The father's salary is respectable and the father's arithmetic is not; within three years the family is moved to London, and within twelve the whole apparatus of respectability has come down on top of him. Portsmouth keeps the house. In 2014, against a will that forbade any monument, the city sets a bronze of him a kilometre south of it, an open book across his knee.
suggested_refs: The Charles Dickens Birthplace Museum, 393 Old Commercial Road, Portsmouth
Martin Jennings's bronze in Guildhall Square, unveiled 7 February 2014, the first Dickens statue on British soil
sources: ITV News, 'Charles Dickens statue unveiled in Portsmouth', 7 February 2014
Atlas Obscura, 'Charles Dickens Statue in Portsmouth'

stops.name: Chatham, Ordnance Terrace and the school of William Giles
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1817 in the Letters Project chronology; the day is a placeholder. Giles's school is dated 1821 in the same chronology and is folded into this stop. The Ordnance Terrace coordinates were not re-fetched from a primary gazetteer this pass.
stops.campa: The Navy Pay Office posts John Dickens to the dockyard at Chatham and the family takes a house in Ordnance Terrace above the town. For five years the boy has the Medway, the marshes, the prison hulks lying off the mud, and the Dover road running out past Gad's Hill. He is small, often ill, and works through his father's shelf of novels twice over. William Giles, a Baptist minister's son, keeps a school here and teaches him from 1821; it is very nearly the whole of his formal education. The family leaves Chatham in 1822, John Dickens no longer able to afford the place, and the boy travels up to London alone in the coach.
suggested_refs: Ordnance Terrace, Chatham, and the Medway dockyard of the 1817-1822 posting
The prison hulks of the Medway, transposed to the opening chapters of Great Expectations

stops.name: Bayham Street, Camden Town: the brass plate
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Camden Town residence 1822-1823 and the Gower Street North move of December 1823 are standard biographical chronology relayed through the dossier and were not confirmed against a fetched source this pass. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The Chatham posting ends and the family comes back to London, to a small house in Bayham Street, Camden Town, with a washerwoman next door and a Bow Street officer opposite. There is no school for Charles now. He runs errands, blacks boots, minds the younger children, and walks the four miles into the city and back, learning the streets by the sole of his shoe. The following winter they move again, to Gower Street North, where Elizabeth Dickens hangs out a brass plate advertising a school for young ladies. Not one pupil ever comes.
suggested_refs: 16 Bayham Street, Camden Town, and 4 Gower Street North, the two addresses of the family's slide into debt
sources: Standard biographical chronology relayed via the research dossier; not independently fetched

stops.name: Hungerford Stairs, the blacking warehouse
stops.date_confidence: attested to late January or early February 1824 in the Letters Project chronology. The stairs themselves are gone under Charing Cross and the Embankment; the pin is approximate to their site and was not re-derived from a survey this pass.
stops.campa: James Lamert, a family connection with a share in the business, offers to take the boy on at Jonathan Warren's blacking warehouse by Hungerford Stairs, a crazy tumbledown place on the river with rats in the cellars. He is twelve. Six shillings a week to cover pots of paste-blacking with oil-paper and then blue paper, tie them, trim them round, and paste on the printed label. He is set to work in the window, where the passers-by can stop and watch him do it. Nobody at Warren's knows he can construe Latin, and he tells nobody.
stops.quote: No words can express the secret agony of my soul as I sunk into this companionship; compared these every-day associates with those of my happier childhood; and felt my early hopes of growing up to be a learned and distinguished man, crushed in my breast.
stops.quote_source: Dickens's autobiographical fragment, written c. mid-1840s and given to John Forster, quoted verbatim in The Life of Charles Dickens
suggested_refs: Dickens's autobiographical fragment, surviving only in the transcription made by John Forster
sources: John Forster, The Life of Charles Dickens, Project Gutenberg 25851

stops.name: Marshalsea Prison, Southwark: the father inside
stops.date_confidence: attested; committal 20 February 1824 and release 28 May 1824 both in the Letters Project chronology. Coordinates are those of the surviving Marshalsea wall on Angel Place.
stops.campa: Twelve days after the boy starts at the warehouse his father is arrested at a baker's suit and committed to the Marshalsea in Southwark. Elizabeth and the younger children move into the prison with him, which the rules allow; Charles does not, because Charles is earning. He walks over the bridge to breakfast with them and back to the blacking. On the twenty-eighth of May a legacy from his grandmother and a Navy Pay Office pension clear the debt and John Dickens walks out. His son stays at the warehouse another ten months.
stops.quote: 'My other piece of advice, Copperfield,' said Mr. Micawber, 'you know. Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure nineteen nineteen and six, result happiness. Annual income twenty pounds, annual expenditure twenty pounds ought and six, result misery.'
stops.quote_source: David Copperfield, Chapter 12, Project Gutenberg 766, verified verbatim against the primary text
suggested_refs: The surviving south wall of the Marshalsea on Angel Place, Southwark
Little Dorrit, whose heroine is born inside this prison
sources: Wikipedia, 'Marshalsea'; Open Plaques; London Guided Walks

stops.name: Lant Street, the back attic
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Lant Street lodging is standard chronology after Forster and is dated only to 1824 in the dossier. Month and day are placeholders to order the segment.
stops.campa: He is lodged first out at Camden and then, to be nearer the prison, in a back attic in Lant Street in the Borough, kept by a family whom the record barely names. He is a boy of twelve living alone on six shillings a week, dividing bread and cheese against the end of it, sometimes not eating at all. He asks his father, in the end, to be lodged nearer the prison, and is. In Pickwick he will hand Lant Street over to Bob Sawyer and call the repose of its inhabitants of a soothing kind.
suggested_refs: Lant Street, Borough, given to Bob Sawyer's lodgings in The Pickwick Papers
sources: Standard chronology after Forster, relayed via the research dossier; not independently fetched

stops.name: Wellington House Academy, Hampstead Road
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Letters Project chronology dates John Dickens's retirement on pension to 9 March 1825 and shows the blacking employment running into March or April of that year, against popular accounts that end it with the imprisonment in May 1824. The school's coordinates were not re-fetched this pass.
stops.campa: John Dickens retires from the Navy Pay Office on a pension, quarrels with Lamert, and takes his son out of the warehouse. Elizabeth, the boy will record and never quite forgive, was warm for his going back. He is sent instead to Wellington House Academy on the Hampstead Road, a school with a savage usher and white mice living in the boys' desks, and stays two years. The blacking is never mentioned in the family again, and he tells nobody else for twenty years, until he writes it down for Forster.
stops.quote: It is wonderful to me how I could have been so easily cast away at such an age. It is wonderful to me that, even after my descent into the poor little drudge I had been since we came to London, no one had compassion enough on me, a child of singular abilities, quick, eager, delicate, and soon hurt, bodily or mentally.
stops.quote_source: Dickens's autobiographical fragment, quoted in John Forster, The Life of Charles Dickens (punctuation of the interpolated clause regularised from Forster's dashes)
suggested_refs: Wellington House Academy, whose usher is reworked into the schoolmasters of Nicholas Nickleby and David Copperfield
sources: John Forster, The Life of Charles Dickens, Project Gutenberg 25851

segments.name: Shorthand: the Law, the Commons, the Gallery

stops.name: Gray's Inn, the copying desk at Ellis and Blackmore
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1827 in the Letters Project chronology, which gives no month; May 1827 to November 1828 is Wikipedia's dating and the standard one. The dossier's chronology lens carried 'March 1827', which its own cited source does not support, and that reading is rejected here. Coordinates are Gray's Inn proper, not the point 250 metres north carried in the dossier.
stops.campa: At fifteen he is put to a desk at Ellis and Blackmore, attorneys of Gray's Inn, as a junior clerk on thirteen shillings and sixpence a week. He copies, he serves papers, he carries money to the courts, and he waits in outer offices, watching the profession from the exact height at which its clients are made to wait. The attorneys of Pickwick and the Chancery suit of Bleak House, which eats a whole estate before it ends, come out of these rooms and out of the eighteen months he spends in them. He leaves in November of the following year.
suggested_refs: Gray's Inn, and the offices of Ellis and Blackmore, attorneys

stops.name: Doctors' Commons, reporting by the folio
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1829 in the Letters Project chronology, which gives no month; day and month are placeholders. The Maria Beadnell attachment is dated May 1830 in the same chronology and is folded into this stop rather than given a pin of its own, since no address for the Beadnell house was verified this pass.
stops.campa: He teaches himself Gurney's shorthand out of a manual and takes a place as a freelance reporter in Doctors' Commons, the ecclesiastical and admiralty courts near St Paul's, where wills are proved and marriages annulled and the work is paid by the folio. It is slow, ill-lit, and profitable enough. From the Commons he is taken into the parliamentary gallery, and from the gallery into print. In these same years he falls in love with Maria Beadnell, a banker's daughter whose family sees a reporter and discourages him for three years until she ends it.
suggested_refs: Doctors' Commons, dissolved 1857, and its proctors, satirised in David Copperfield
Maria Beadnell, reappearing as Dora Spenlow and, twenty-five years later, as Flora Finching

stops.name: The British Museum, a reader's ticket at eighteen
stops.date_confidence: attested; 8 February 1830 in the Letters Project chronology, the day after his eighteenth birthday. Coordinates are the standard British Museum pin and were not re-fetched for this specific fact.
stops.campa: The day after his eighteenth birthday, the earliest age the rules allow, he applies for and is granted a reader's ticket at the British Museum. He has had perhaps four years of schooling in his life. No university will ever have him and no university will ever be asked. He works through Shakespeare, Goldsmith, Addison, Berkeley, and a history of England, alone, in the Reading Room, in the hours between reporting shifts. Asked in later life where he had been educated, he named this room and the streets outside it.
suggested_refs: The British Museum Reading Room register, February 1830

stops.name: Furnival's Inn, the first number of Pickwick
stops.date_confidence: attested; Sketches by Boz, First Series, published 8 February 1836 and the first Pickwick number 31 March 1836, both per the Letters Project. Seymour's death on 20 April 1836 is attested; the claim that Dickens drove him to it is contested and is not made here. The Furnival's Inn coordinates were not re-fetched this pass.
stops.campa: From chambers at Furnival's Inn in Holborn, a parliamentary reporter for the Morning Chronicle publishes sketches over the name Boz, collects them in February in a volume illustrated by George Cruikshank, and on the last day of March issues the first monthly number of The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club. Robert Seymour, the illustrator whose sporting notion began the whole scheme, quarrels with the writer over its direction and shoots himself three weeks later. Sales are slow until Sam Weller enters in the fourth number; by the end of the run the monthly parts are selling forty thousand.
suggested_refs: Seymour's seven Pickwick plates, and the succession to Hablot Knight Browne
'A Madman's Manuscript', a Pickwick chapter, translated into Spanish in the Cadiz periodical El Pasatiempo in 1844, the earliest known direct rendering of any Dickens text from English into Spanish
sources: University of Barcelona, 'UB researcher finds the first Spanish translation of a Dickens' text' (2021)

stops.name: St Luke's, Chelsea: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested; 2 April 1836 in the Letters Project chronology. The honeymoon week at Chalk is standard biography and was not fetched this pass.
stops.campa: Two days after the first Pickwick number he marries Catherine Thomson Hogarth at St Luke's in Chelsea, daughter of George Hogarth, a fellow journalist who had commissioned work from him. He is twenty-four. They will have ten children and separate after twenty-two years, and her two younger sisters, Mary and Georgina, will each in turn come to live in his house. The wedding is small, and the honeymoon is one week at Chalk in Kent, because the second number of Pickwick falls due.
suggested_refs: St Luke's Church, Chelsea, and the Hogarth family of the Morning Chronicle

segments.name: Doughty Street and the Making of Boz

stops.name: 48 Doughty Street, the parish boy and the gruel
stops.date_confidence: attested; tenancy 25 March 1837 to December 1839 per Wikipedia's Charles Dickens Museum article. Coordinates unified here on 51.5239, -0.1169 from that article; the dossier carried three different pairs for this one address. Note also an unreconciled conflict in the dossier over which books belong to the house, one lens saying Oliver Twist and Nicholas Nickleby, another Oliver Twist and the end of Pickwick. Both are in fact true and neither list is complete.
stops.campa: He takes a lease on a twelve-room house in Doughty Street, a private road with a gate and a porter at either end, the first address of his life that announces money. Catherine is pregnant. Mary Hogarth, seventeen, moves in with them. He is editing Bentley's Miscellany, finishing Pickwick, and beginning Oliver Twist in the same months. Nobody in the house has heard of Hungerford Stairs. In the second chapter of the new book a parish boy raised on thin gruel gets up from the table with his basin in his hand and walks the length of the workhouse hall to the master.
stops.quote: Please, sir, I want some more.
stops.quote_source: Oliver Twist, Chapter II, Project Gutenberg 730
suggested_refs: 48 Doughty Street, saved from demolition by the Dickens Fellowship in 1924 and opened as the Charles Dickens Museum in 1925
sources: Charles Dickens Museum, 'Dickens in Doughty Street: 100 Years of the Charles Dickens Museum'

stops.name: 48 Doughty Street, Mary Hogarth dies
stops.date_confidence: attested; 7 May 1837 per the Letters Project chronology and standard biography after Forster. The suspension of both serials for a month is attested in the same chronology.
stops.campa: They come back from the theatre late on a Saturday evening. Mary Hogarth goes up to her room, is taken ill in the night, and dies the following afternoon, seventeen years old. Nothing in the letters records grief of this order for anyone else he loses, not his father, not his own daughter. Dying girls will keep entering his novels; Little Nell is four years away. For the only time in his working life the machine stops, and the month's numbers of Pickwick and of Oliver Twist do not appear.
suggested_refs: Mary Scott Hogarth's grave at Kensal Green, and the epitaph Dickens wrote for it
sources: John Forster, The Life of Charles Dickens

stops.name: Bowes, the Yorkshire school
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on the specific attribution; the Yorkshire journey of late January to early February 1838 with Hablot Browne is standard chronology, and Wikipedia's Bowes article confirms the village as the model for Dotheboys Hall and names George Ashton Taylor's grave there as the model for Smike, but it does not name William Shaw's academy or supply a date. Coordinates corrected to the village itself. Bowes is in County Durham today; it was in the North Riding of Yorkshire in 1838, which is why the schools were called Yorkshire schools.
stops.campa: He travels north in the last days of January with Hablot Browne, both men under false names and carrying a letter of introduction invented for the purpose, to look at the cheap boarding schools where unwanted boys are sent and forgotten at twenty guineas a year, no vacations, no questions. What he finds at Bowes goes into Nicholas Nickleby as Dotheboys Hall and Wackford Squeers. In the churchyard lies George Ashton Taylor, a pupil dead at nineteen, whose stone he reads and who becomes Smike. Within a few years of the novel the Yorkshire schools begin to close.
suggested_refs: The churchyard at Bowes and the grave of George Ashton Taylor, died 1822 aged 19
sources: Standard chronology of the 1838 Yorkshire journey relayed via the research dossier

stops.name: 1 Devonshire Terrace, the Curiosity Shop years
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the tenancy from late 1839 to 1851 is standard chronology relayed via the dossier and was not confirmed against a fetched source. Master Humphrey's Clock launched 4 April 1840 per the Letters Project; the fistula operation is dated only to 1841 in the same chronology. Day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He moves his household to a large house near Regent's Park with a garden and a coach house, and stays eleven years. Nicholas Nickleby, Barnaby Rudge, the American journey, the Christmas books, and the birth and death of his daughter Dora all belong to this address. Master Humphrey's Clock starts here in April 1840 and turns into the vehicle for The Old Curiosity Shop, whose readers write to him from both sides of the Atlantic begging for Nell's life. In 1841 he is cut for an anal fistula on a table in this house, without anaesthetic, and goes back to work.
suggested_refs: Master Humphrey's Clock, weekly, 1840-1841

The transatlantic reader mail over the death of Little Nell; the pier-side scene at New York, in which crowds are said to have shouted 'Is Little Nell dead?' at an incoming ship, is a reception legend later biographers class as unverifiable in that exact form
sources: Standard chronology relayed via the research dossier

stops.name: Boston, the Britannia lands
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1842 in the Letters Project chronology; the day is a placeholder, no arrival date having been verified this pass.
stops.campa: He lands at Boston in January, twenty-nine years old, the most widely read writer in the English-speaking world and the first to arrive in America as a celebrity rather than a visitor. Crowds meet the ship. He is dined, followed, printed, and quoted, and within a few weeks he begins saying in public what he came to say: that American houses reprint his books without paying him a penny, that an international copyright is a matter of plain honesty, and that he intends to keep raising it. The American press turns on him for it.
suggested_refs: American Notes for General Circulation (1842)
The international copyright petition Dickens carried, signed by British authors
sources: American Notes for General Circulation (1842), Project Gutenberg 675

stops.name: Eastern State Penitentiary, Philadelphia: the separate system
stops.date_confidence: attested; the 8 March 1842 visit date is given by Eastern State Penitentiary's own history pages and by the Victorian Web excerpt of American Notes. Coordinates 2027 Fairmount Avenue.
stops.campa: He spends a full day inside the Philadelphia penitentiary, going cell to cell with the officers and sitting down with men held under the separate system, hooded on arrival so that no other prisoner ever sees their faces, then kept alone for years. The keepers show it to him as reform, humane where the lash is not, and are proud enough of it to walk a famous novelist through the whole building. He leaves convinced that the men in those cells are being taken apart in a way that leaves no mark on the body, and says nothing of it to the keepers who have shown him round. American Notes is out before the year ends.
stops.quote: I hold this slow and daily tampering with the mysteries of the brain, to be immeasurably worse than any torture of the body.
stops.quote_source: American Notes for General Circulation (1842), Chapter VII, 'Philadelphia, and its Solitary Prison'
suggested_refs: American Notes, Chapter VII, on the Philadelphia separate system
sources: American Notes for General Circulation (1842), via Victorian Web

stops.name: Philadelphia, Poe at the United States Hotel
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The meeting is documented in Dickens and Poe biography but appears nowhere in edgar_allan_poe.journey.json and is not in this subject's own dossier, which never mentions Poe. The dossier's interlock lens dates it only to March 1842; the day here is assigned to order the Philadelphia stay and carries no authority. Coordinates are the canonical Philadelphia pin inherited from Poe's own file.
stops.campa: Edgar Allan Poe, in the middle of his Philadelphia years and working for Graham's Magazine, writes asking for an interview and is granted one at the United States Hotel. Poe presses a volume of his tales on the visitor, who promises to try it on English publishers, tries, and fails, and writes afterwards to say so. Poe had already reviewed Barnaby Rudge and boasted in print of having guessed its ending from the early instalments. They meet twice, two men who both live by the number and the deadline. What was said at the second interview nobody wrote down.
suggested_refs: Poe's review of Barnaby Rudge in Graham's Magazine, February 1842
The five Poe addresses in Philadelphia, 1838-1844
sources: edgar_allan_poe.journey.json (Philadelphia pin only; the meeting is not recorded there)
Standard Dickens and Poe biography; not independently fetched this pass

stops.name: Washington, President Tyler and the copyright question
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the dossier dates the Washington leg only to March 1842 and did not fetch a source for it. The day is assigned to order the itinerary. The Tyler meeting is standard 1842 itinerary and is not independently confirmed here.
stops.campa: He is received at the White House by John Tyler, an accidental president with a hostile Congress. Here as in every other city he raises international copyright and is told, courteously and then less so, that a free people have a right to cheap books. Here too, in the capital of the republic he came out prepared to admire, he sees slavery at close quarters for the first time. He had crossed as a radical and rather more than half a republican. In the galleries of both chambers he sits and watches the legislators of that republic spit tobacco onto the carpet.
suggested_refs: American Notes, Chapter VIII, on Washington and the Capitol
sources: Standard 1842 itinerary relayed via the research dossier; not independently fetched

stops.name: Richmond, the turning point south
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the dossier dates the Richmond leg only to March 1842 and did not fetch a source. The day is assigned to order the itinerary. The quote is verified verbatim, but its attribution has been corrected: it stands in Chapter III, 'Boston', not in a dedicatory epistle to Dr Channing, American Notes having no such dedication.
stops.campa: He goes south as far as Richmond and turns back, unwilling to go further into slaveholding country. He has seen the auction advertisements, the hired-out house servants, the iron collar. In American Notes he gives slavery an entire chapter and fills much of it with runaway notices clipped from Southern newspapers and reprinted without comment: the scars, the brands, the missing teeth, the bullet still in the leg, each detail entered by an owner as a means of identification. He sets them in columns, page after page, with nothing of his own put in between them.
stops.quote: that most hideous blot and foul disgrace—Slavery
stops.quote_source: American Notes for General Circulation (1842), Chapter III, 'Boston', Project Gutenberg 675 (verbatim, including the original dash)
suggested_refs: American Notes, Chapter XVII, 'Slavery'
sources: American Notes for General Circulation (1842), Project Gutenberg 675
Standard 1842 itinerary relayed via the research dossier

stops.name: Niagara Falls, the one unguarded page
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the standard itinerary puts the arrival at 26 April 1842 with a stay of roughly ten days into early May, so the dossier's flat 'May 1842' misses the arrival. Wikipedia's American Notes article confirms the Great Lakes leg but gives no day-level dates. Coordinates are the city of Niagara Falls, Ontario; Horseshoe Falls itself lies at 43.0779, -79.0747.
stops.campa: He reaches the falls at the end of April and stays about ten days, crossing to the Canadian side and going down to the foot of the Horseshoe with the spray soaking through everything he has on. Nothing else on the continent takes him this way. The pages he gives it in American Notes are the only entirely unguarded ones in the book, written by a man who has spent four months being furious in public and has finally arrived at something about which he is not required to have an opinion. In two weeks he sails for home.
suggested_refs: American Notes, Chapter XIV, on Niagara
sources: Standard 1842 itinerary relayed via the research dossier

segments.name: The Carol, Genoa, and the Continental Years

stops.name: Field Lane Ragged School, Saffron Hill
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the September 1843 visit and its link to the Burdett-Coutts correspondence are stated in the dossier and were not independently fetched. Coordinates are approximate to Saffron Hill. The day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He goes down to Saffron Hill, into a set of rooms above a slaughterhouse where volunteers teach the alphabet to children no ordinary schoolroom will take: thieves, crossing-sweepers, boys who have never once slept indoors. He writes about it to Angela Burdett-Coutts, and to the editor of the Edinburgh Review, and turns over the idea of a pamphlet on behalf of the poor man's child. He decides against the pamphlet. The thing he writes that autumn instead is a ghost story with a rich man in it and a crippled child.
suggested_refs: The Field Lane Ragged School, Saffron Hill, and Dickens's 1843 letters on it to Angela Burdett-Coutts
Ignorance and Want, the two children shown under the Ghost of Christmas Present's robe
sources: Research dossier, citing the Burdett-Coutts correspondence; not independently fetched

stops.name: 1 Devonshire Terrace, A Christmas Carol
stops.date_confidence: attested; publication 19 December 1843 and the approximate 6,000 copies sold before Christmas per the Letters Project chronology and the Charles Dickens Museum's publication history. The piracy suit and its costs are standard publication history and were not fetched this pass.
stops.campa: He writes it in six weeks in the autumn, walking the black streets of London fifteen and twenty miles at a stretch by night, and pays for the production out of his own pocket: gilt edges, hand-coloured plates, cloth binding, five shillings, cheap enough that anyone can have it. Six thousand copies go before Christmas and the profit is a fraction of what he had counted on, because he has made the book too handsome to earn. Within two months it is being pirated. He sues, wins, and recovers nothing, the pirates having gone bankrupt, and pays the costs himself.
stops.quote_source: A Christmas Carol, Stave One, Project Gutenberg 46
suggested_refs: A Christmas Carol, first edition, Chapman and Hall, December 1843, with John Leech's hand-coloured plates

stops.name: Palazzo delle Peschiere, Genoa: the mesmerist
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move to Genoa on 16 July 1844 per the Letters Project; the Peschiere tenancy is corrected here to late September 1844 through June 1845, the family having first taken the Villa Bagnerello at Albaro. The Italian Wikipedia page for the palazzo returned 404 this pass, so the coordinates rest on the dossier and are unconfirmed. The training under John Elliotson is standard biography, not fetched.
stops.campa: After a summer in a villa out at Albaro the family moves into the Palazzo delle Peschiere above the city, with its painted hall, its fish ponds, and its view down over the harbour. He learns Italian, walks the alleys, and begins mesmerising Emile de la Rue's English wife Augusta, who suffers convulsions and is followed everywhere, she says, by a phantom figure. The animal magnetism he is using is Franz Mesmer's, seventy years on, learned in London from the physician John Elliotson. He puts her under daily for months and keeps notes. Catherine, watching, makes a quarrel of it that lasts years.
suggested_refs: Pictures from Italy (1846)
Dickens's letters to Emile de la Rue on the mesmeric treatment of his wife
mesmer.journey.json, for the origin of the animal magnetism Dickens is practising here
sources: Standard Dickens biography drawing on the de la Rue correspondence

stops.name: Rosemont, Lausanne: Dombey without streets
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Lausanne residence is standard chronology relayed via the dossier and unconfirmed by a fetched source. The Daily News editorship is attested and precisely dated by the Letters Project, 21 January to 9 February 1846, and is folded into this stop. Day and month of the Lausanne arrival are placeholders.
stops.campa: He takes a small villa above the lake at Lausanne, having spent three weeks in January founding the Daily News and then resigning the editorship of it, and sits down to write Dombey and Son. The work goes badly and he blames the town: no streets. He needs crowds, gas, and noise at his elbow to write, and the absence of London is a physical want he complains of in letter after letter. He visits the blind institution and climbs to the hospice on the Great St Bernard. The first numbers of Dombey go off to London on time.
suggested_refs: Villa Rosemont, Lausanne
The Daily News, founded January 1846, editorship resigned 9 February
sources: Standard chronology relayed via the research dossier

stops.name: Paris, the winter house in the Rue de Courcelles
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the 1846-1847 Paris winter is standard chronology relayed via the dossier and unconfirmed by a fetched source. The call on Victor Hugo in the Place Royale is standard Dickens biography and is not in the dossier at all; it is carried here as reconstruction. Coordinates are the canonical Paris pin.
stops.campa: The household moves on to Paris for the winter and takes a house in the Rue de Courcelles that he describes as the most preposterous in the world, all mirrors and hangings and rooms giving on rooms. He works at Dombey, walks the city by night as he walks London, visits the morgue more than once, and calls on Victor Hugo at his apartment in the Place Royale. He will come back to Paris repeatedly for the rest of his life, and some of the crossings of the early eighteen-sixties are read by biographers as journeys made for Ellen Ternan rather than for France.
suggested_refs: The Paris morgue, revisited in The Uncommercial Traveller

stops.name: Urania Cottage, Shepherd's Bush
stops.date_confidence: attested for the founding year, corrected from the dossier's 1846: Wikipedia's Urania Cottage article gives 1847, the home opening in November of that year. Dickens's own involvement ends in 1858 with the separation; the institution itself continued some years afterwards, so the 1858 terminus belongs to him, not to the house. Coordinates were not re-fetched this pass.
stops.campa: With Angela Burdett-Coutts's money and his own hand on every detail he opens a home in Shepherd's Bush, then still fields and market gardens, for women coming out of prison, the streets, and the workhouse. He interviews the applicants himself, writes the rules, chooses the furniture and the printed cotton for the dresses, and invents a marks system by which a woman builds her own record week by week. The end of it is emigration: Australia, the Cape, a passage and a character. He runs it for eleven years, until the separation of 1858 takes him out of it.
suggested_refs: Urania Cottage, Lime Grove, Shepherd's Bush, later absorbed into Gaumont's Lime Grove Studios

stops.name: Fort House, Broadstairs: the table facing the North Sea
stops.date_confidence: attested for the house and the coordinates, 51.3598N 1.4450E per Wikipedia and the Historic England listing. Two dossier claims are corrected: the lease ran from the 1840s to 1852, not 1837-1859, and the novel written here was David Copperfield, not Bleak House, the renaming being an early twentieth-century attribution the article itself calls disputed. Bleak House was written at Tavistock House in 1852-1853. Day and month are placeholders for the 1849 working summer.
stops.campa: He has been coming to Broadstairs since he was twenty-five, and through the eighteen-forties he leases the flint house on the cliff above Viking Bay, working at a table facing the North Sea with the fleet going by under the window. Here he writes David Copperfield, the book in which the blacking warehouse finally surfaces, disguised as a wine merchant's cellar and handed to a boy whose initials are his own reversed. Half a century later the house is renamed Bleak House on an attribution that is almost certainly wrong.
stops.quote: Whether I shall turn out to be the hero of my own life, or whether that station will be held by anybody else, these pages must show.
stops.quote_source: David Copperfield, Chapter I, opening sentence, Project Gutenberg 766
suggested_refs: Fort House, Broadstairs, Historic England listing
Bonchurch, Isle of Wight, another of the 1849 Copperfield summers

stops.name: London, Household Words begins
stops.date_confidence: attested; launch 30 March 1850 per the Letters Project chronology and Dickens Journals Online. The stop is pinned at Devonshire Terrace, his residence at the time, rather than at the Wellington Street office, for which no coordinate was verified this pass.
stops.campa: He starts a twopenny weekly of his own, with the words conducted by Charles Dickens standing at the head of every page and every column, and runs it for nine years. Reportage on sewers, sanitation, ragged schools, patent law, workhouses and factory accidents is printed alongside fiction, and nothing in it is signed. Nothing appears in it that he has not read first. He is now proprietor, editor, and the best-selling novelist in England at once. Hard Times will be written into it to lift the circulation.
suggested_refs: Household Words, 1850-1859, complete run at Dickens Journals Online

stops.name: 1 Devonshire Terrace, the father and the infant
stops.date_confidence: attested; John Dickens died 31 March 1851 and Dora Annie Dickens on 14 April 1851, aged eight months, both per the Letters Project chronology. The account of the operation on John Dickens is standard biography drawn from Dickens's own letters and was not fetched this pass.
stops.campa: John Dickens dies at the end of March after an operation for a bladder complaint carried out without anaesthetic, which his son describes afterwards as the most terrible operation known to surgery. Two weeks later, on the fourteenth of April, Charles is thirty-nine and on his feet speaking at a public dinner when word is brought that his eight-month-old daughter Dora has died at home that evening. It is the last spring the family spends in this house. He goes back through the dark to a dead child upstairs and a wife who has still to be told.
suggested_refs: Dora Annie Dickens, born August 1850, died 14 April 1851

stops.name: Tavistock House, the dummy books on the study door
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the 1851-1860 tenancy is standard chronology relayed via the dossier and unconfirmed by a fetched source. The dummy book-backs and the schoolroom theatricals are standard biography. Day and month are placeholders.
stops.campa: He buys the remainder of a lease on an eighteen-room house at the corner of Tavistock Square, has the whole interior rebuilt to his own specification, and fits the study door with dummy book-backs bearing titles he invents himself: Hansard's Guide to Refreshing Sleep, a History of a Short Chancery Suit in twenty volumes. Bleak House, Hard Times, Little Dorrit and A Tale of Two Cities are written in this room. In the schoolroom he builds a stage and mounts plays on it with the children, the servants, and Wilkie Collins.
suggested_refs: Tavistock House, demolished 1901; the dummy book-backs survive at Gad's Hill

stops.name: Preston, the seventh month of the lockout
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the dossier dates the visit to January 1854 and its bearing on Hard Times, but the entry was not independently re-fetched. The day is assigned to order the segment and carries no authority. The strike-committee details are standard accounts of the Preston lockout and are relayed rather than verified here.
stops.campa: He goes north to Preston in the seventh month of a cotton lockout, twenty-five thousand hands out of work, and sits through a delegates' meeting in a chapel. What he finds is order: minutes read out, subscriptions from other towns acknowledged one by one, no rioting, no drunkenness, a hall of men conducting their own affairs a good deal better than most parish vestries conduct theirs. He also finds an outside agitator he mistrusts on sight and puts straight into a novel as Slackbridge. He writes the visit up for Household Words on the eleventh of February. Hard Times comes out of this fortnight.
suggested_refs: 'On Strike', Household Words, 11 February 1854, Dickens's own account of the Preston visit

stops.name: Gad's Hill Place, the house from the road
stops.date_confidence: attested; purchase March 1856 for 1,790 pounds per the Letters Project and Wikipedia's Gad's Hill Place article. Coordinates corrected: the dossier carried three different pairs for this one house across its three lenses, two of them several kilometres out. All Gad's Hill stops in this file are unified on 51.4112, 0.4579 per Wikipedia. The childhood promise on the road is traditional, resting on Forster. The day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He buys the house he used to be walked past as a small boy on the Rochester road, when his father told him that if he worked hard enough he might come to live in it. One thousand seven hundred and ninety pounds. It stands at the top of Gad's Hill on the Dover road, where Falstaff robbed the travellers and ran away, and the marsh country where Pip meets his convict lies a few miles off across the fields. The Kent of his childhood is now an address he owns. He lets the house out at first and moves in himself in June 1857.
stops.quote: My father's family name being Pirrip, and my Christian name Philip, my infant tongue could make of both names nothing longer or more explicit than Pip.
stops.quote_source: Great Expectations, Chapter I, opening sentence, Project Gutenberg 1400
suggested_refs: Gad's Hill Place, Higham, now Gad's Hill School, opened to heritage visitors
The Swiss chalet given to Dickens by Charles Fechter and set up in the shrubbery across the road

segments.name: The Frozen Deep and the Breaking of the House

stops.name: Free Trade Hall, Manchester: the Ternans are hired
stops.date_confidence: attested for August 1857 and the hiring of the Ternans per standard biography drawing on correspondence and Ternan family papers; the identification of the Free Trade Hall as the venue is relayed via the dossier and was not independently fetched, and the day is assigned to order the segment.
stops.campa: He takes Wilkie Collins's melodrama The Frozen Deep to Manchester for three performances in a hall seating two thousand, far too large for the amateur ladies of his own household, and hires professionals to replace them: Frances Ternan and her daughters Maria and Ellen. He plays Richard Wardour, who dies saving his rival, and is carried offstage each night to audible weeping. He is forty-five. Ellen Ternan is eighteen. Within nine months a marriage of twenty-two years is over, and whatever replaces it is never once written down.
suggested_refs: Wilkie Collins, The Frozen Deep (1856), written for Dickens's Tavistock House theatricals

stops.name: Tavistock House, the Personal statement
stops.date_confidence: attested, with a correction. The Letters Project reads '(7 and 12 June) publishes "Personal" statement about it', two dates; Wikipedia's Catherine Dickens article pins the Household Words appearance to 12 June and records that the statement went first to the newspapers, The Times among them. The dossier had the two publications the wrong way round and is corrected here. The separation terms of roughly 600 pounds a year are commonly given but rest on secondary accounts.
stops.campa: Catherine leaves for a house in Gloucester Crescent with six hundred a year and one son; the other children stay with their father under Georgina Hogarth's management. London talk names Ellen Ternan, and then, more viciously, Georgina. He answers the way a proprietor answers, in print: a statement sent to the papers and carried by The Times on the seventh of June, then reprinted over his own name in Household Words on the twelfth. Forster begged him not to. Within a year he has shut Household Words, launched All the Year Round in its place, and put A Tale of Two Cities in the first number.
stops.quote: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair.
stops.quote_source: A Tale of Two Cities, opening sentence, Project Gutenberg 98

stops.name: Gad's Hill Place, the bonfire in the field
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1860 in standard biography drawing on witness accounts at Gad's Hill; nothing was found against it this pass. Coordinates corrected as at the purchase stop. The day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: On a September day he has the letters of twenty years carried out into the field behind the house and burned, basket after basket, while the children roast onions in the ashes. Everything anybody had ever written to him goes into it: Thackeray, Carlyle, Wilkie Collins, Angela Burdett-Coutts, his own family. He asks his correspondents to destroy his letters to them in return, and a great many oblige him. What survives of the other side of his correspondence survives because somebody disobeyed.
suggested_refs: The Pilgrim Edition of the Letters of Charles Dickens, twelve volumes, assembled from the surviving outgoing half
sources: Standard Dickens biography drawing on contemporary witness accounts at Gad's Hill

stops.name: St James's Hall, Piccadilly: Sikes and Nancy
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; St James's Hall as a principal London reading venue from 1861 is relayed via the dossier and unconfirmed by a fetched source. The day and month are assigned to order the segment. The pulse figures and the rehearsal count are standard biography and are relayed rather than verified here.
stops.campa: From 1858 he reads his own books for money, and from 1861 he does it mostly here, on a platform of his own design with a maroon screen behind him and the gas jets angled at his face so that nothing of the expression is lost. The Carol, the Trial from Pickwick, Little Dombey, Mrs Gamp. Later he adds Sikes murdering Nancy and rehearses it more than a hundred times before he will risk it; women are carried out of the hall, and his own pulse is taken at seventy-two before and a hundred and twelve after. His doctors tell him to stop.
stops.quote_source: A Christmas Carol, Stave Three, Project Gutenberg 46 (spoken by Tiny Tim)

stops.name: Staplehurst, the Beult viaduct
stops.date_confidence: attested; 9 June 1865 at 3:13 pm, the Beult viaduct, Dickens aged 53 travelling with Ellen Ternan and her mother, all confirmed by Wikipedia's Staplehurst rail crash article and by railwaysarchive.co.uk. Coordinates corrected from the dossier's chronology lens, which sat 1.5 km short of the viaduct in open farmland, and unified on the geography lens's value.
stops.campa: The tidal boat train from Folkestone runs off the viaduct over the river Beult at thirteen minutes past three in the afternoon, a length of rail having been lifted for repairs and the timetable read wrong by the foreman. Ten people die. His carriage hangs off the bridge and does not fall. He climbs out through the window, gets Ellen Ternan and her mother clear, fills his hat from the stream and works for hours down in the wreck with brandy and water for the dying. Then he goes back up into the hanging carriage for the manuscript in his coat pocket.
suggested_refs: Our Mutual Friend, the postscript in lieu of a preface, in which Dickens describes going back for the number

stops.name: Gad's Hill Place, the Eyre subscription
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Dickens's adherence to the Eyre Defence and Aid Committee is stated in the dossier and is standard, but no fetched source was obtained this pass and no attendance by him at a London meeting is attested. The stop is placed at his own residence, from which he subscribed, rather than at a London venue he is not documented as entering. Date is a placeholder to order the segment. Note a corpus gap: john_ruskin.journey.json records nothing of Eyre, Jamaica, or Dickens.
stops.campa: Governor Eyre has put down a rising at Morant Bay in Jamaica with four hundred and thirty-nine executions, six hundred floggings and a thousand houses burned, and England divides over it. The Jamaica Committee, with John Stuart Mill, Charles Darwin and Huxley, moves to have him prosecuted for murder. The Eyre Defence and Aid Committee raises money to defend him, and its subscribers are Carlyle, Tennyson, Kingsley, John Ruskin and Dickens. Twenty-four years earlier, in the chapter of American Notes he gave to slavery, he had reprinted a column of runaway advertisements without a word of his own between them.

stops.name: Tremont Temple, Boston: the second crossing
stops.date_confidence: attested with a correction: the Letters Project reads '(Nov.) begins American reading tour in Boston', Dickens having sailed on 9 November 1867 and landed on the 19th, with the first reading at Tremont Temple on 2 December. The dossier's flat '1867-12' was attributed to a source that says November; both dates are given here and the stop takes the first reading. The profit, just under 20,000 pounds, is the Charles Dickens Museum's estimate and stays attributed to it.
stops.campa: He sails in November, twenty-five years after the first crossing, this time to be paid. Tickets are resold at four and five times their face value and queues sleep in the street outside the halls overnight. He gives seventy-six readings in five months, Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Washington and back again, coughing, sleepless, unable to eat before a performance, carried through the evenings on champagne and beef tea. A foot swells so badly he cannot get a boot on and reads with it bandaged on a stool. The Charles Dickens Museum puts the profit at just under twenty thousand pounds. He sails for England in April.
suggested_refs: Tremont Temple, Boston, first reading 2 December 1867

stops.name: Buckingham Palace, the audience
stops.date_confidence: attested; the audience of 9 March 1870 is recorded in Queen Victoria's own journal as cited in standard Dickens biography. The primary journal entry was not pulled this pass, so the detail of the conversation and the inscription on the presented volume rest on the dossier's sourcing and on general biographical consensus.
stops.campa: The Queen receives him for an hour and a half. She remains standing, as she does with commoners, and so does he. They talk about the price of butcher's meat and of bread, about the difficulty of keeping servants, and about whether the division between the classes in England can ever be got rid of, which she doubts and he does not. He has been offered no title and will accept none. He gives her a set of his books bound in morocco. She gives him her own Leaves from the Journal of Our Life in the Highlands, inscribed from the humblest of writers to one of the greatest.
suggested_refs: Queen Victoria's journal, entry for 9 March 1870, Royal Archives

stops.name: Gad's Hill Place, the couch in the dining room
stops.date_confidence: attested, with the dossier's internal contradiction resolved in favour of its afterlife lens: the collapse was on 8 June 1870 and the death on 9 June, so a single entry stamped 1870-06-09 describing a stroke followed by death 'the next day' could not stand. The Letters Project gives '(9 June) dies, aged 58' and the Abbey gravestone reads the same. Wikipedia places the death 'on a couch in the dining room', against the dossier's geography lens, which had him die at his desk. Coordinates corrected as at the other Gad's Hill stops.
stops.campa: He works all morning on the sixth number of The Mystery of Edwin Drood in the chalet across the road, and again after lunch, which he never does. At dinner with Georgina he says he has been very ill for an hour, asks to be got to London at once, and falls. She gets him onto a couch in the dining room. He never speaks again, and dies at ten past six the following evening, the ninth of June, five years to the day after Staplehurst. Six numbers of twelve exist. In 1873 a Vermont printer publishes the other six, dictated to him, he says, by Dickens.
suggested_refs: The Mystery of Edwin Drood, six numbers, April to September 1870

stops.name: Rochester, the grave that was not used
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction on the date, which is assigned to sit between the death and the burial; the sources give no day for the decision. That Dickens wished for burial in Kent and that a grave was prepared at Rochester before the Abbey campaign overruled it is stated by sdrfoundation.org and medway.gov.uk and relayed via the dossier, without a document being fetched this pass.
stops.campa: He had asked in his will for an inexpensive, unostentatious and strictly private funeral, his name in plain English letters, and no monument, memorial or testimonial whatever. Rochester was to have him. He loved the town, and a grave was dug ready at the cathedral, within sight of the castle and the river he had known since he was five years old. Edwin Drood, unfinished on the desk at Gad's Hill, is set in this town under another name. Then The Times ran a leader saying the Abbey, Dean Stanley agreed, and Forster and the family gave way. The Rochester grave was filled in unused.
suggested_refs: Rochester Cathedral and the churchyard of St Nicholas

stops.name: Poets' Corner, Westminster Abbey
stops.date_confidence: attested; Westminster Abbey's own commemoration page gives 14 June 1870 at 9:30 am and states that only twelve mourners attended, correcting the dossier's fourteen. The same page records the grave being left open through mid-morning on 15 June for the public and closed on 16 June, which complicates the phrase 'strictly private'. Coordinates are the canonical Abbey pin already carried by charles_darwin.journey.json, bulwer_lytton.journey.json, edward_burne_jones.journey.json and max_muller.journey.json.
stops.campa: A special train brings the coffin up from Higham and the funeral is held at half past nine in the morning with twelve people present: three plain carriages, no plumes, no black bows, no scarves, nothing announced beforehand. That much of the will is honoured. The location is not. The grave is left open through the next day and the day after, and thousands file past it and drop flowers in until it is closed on the sixteenth. The stone set into the floor of Poets' Corner carries his name and two dates and nothing else at all.
suggested_refs: Westminster Abbey, Poets' Corner, near the monuments to Chaucer and Handel
